solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Argue with Republican approach (7)

blocks.note: an angle = an approach to a problem

annotation.surface: Someone is urged to take on a Republican's approach in an argument.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Argue with' reads as one phrase, but 'with' belongs to the wordplay as W, leaving 'Argue' alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: To wrangle is to argue at length, often noisily.

entries.clue: One signalling game is up? (7-6)

blocks.note: read as a referee raising a hand or a flag, and meant as someone tipping off the authorities
read as the final whistle of a match, and meant as 'your scheme has been found out'

annotation.surface: A referee blows the whistle to signal the end of a game.
annotation.walkthrough: The picture is a referee ending a match; the real sense is an informer, whose tip-off tells wrongdoers 'the game is up'.
annotation.definitionFit: A whistle-blower exposes wrongdoing, signalling to the culprits that their game is up.

entries.clue: Release loaves bishop ordered (7)

indicatorNotes.ordered: the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: B = bishop, as in chess notation

annotation.surface: A bishop places an order for bread to be released.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ordered' looks like the bishop buying bread, but it tells you to rearrange LOAVES and B.
annotation.definitionFit: To absolve is to release someone from guilt or obligation.

entries.clue: Kind of setter for one to turn up (5)

indicatorNotes.to turn up: in a down clue, turning up reads the letters bottom to top

blocks.note: the sun is something that sets
reversal indicator: in a down clue, turning up reads SUN + EG from the bottom

annotation.surface: A puzzle-maker of some sort is waiting for someone to arrive.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Setter' in a crossword wants to be the compiler; here it is the sun, which sets every evening.
annotation.definitionFit: A genus is a kind or class, especially in biology.

entries.clue: Questioned dictator caught in river delta (8)

indicatorNotes.caught in: the dictator is trapped inside the river and delta

blocks.note: the Exe, a river in Devon; AMIN goes between EX and E
D = delta in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: A captured dictator is interrogated in the delta of a river.
annotation.walkthrough: The dictator goes inside the river, not the delta; D is simply added at the end. Idi Amin ruled Uganda in the 1970s.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: a witness who has been questioned in court has been examined.

entries.clue: The Speaker’s course of action is plain (6)

indicatorNotes.The Speaker’s: what the speaker says is heard, not seen

blocks.note: a step is a measure or course of action

annotation.surface: The Commons Speaker's intended course of action is clear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Speaker' suggests the chair of the House of Commons, and 'plain' reads as 'obvious'; it is really a flat grassland.
annotation.definitionFit: A steppe is a vast treeless plain, as in Central Asia.

entries.clue: Be careful, young man? (6)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Be careful' is an imperative, matching the exclamation 'Steady!'; 'young man' matches the noun, a regular boyfriend

blocks.note: an exclamation of warning, like 'Easy now!'
a regular boyfriend; the question mark flags a young man as just one example

annotation.surface: An older person warns a young man to take care.
annotation.walkthrough: It reads as one warning addressed to a youth; split it after the comma and 'young man' becomes a boyfriend, someone's steady.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Steady!' warns someone to take care, and a steady is a regular sweetheart.

entries.clue: Duke’s wife expelled from capital (9)

indicatorNotes.expelled from: the wife is thrown out of the capital's name

annotation.surface: A duke's wife is thrown out of the capital.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Duke's' looks like a British nobleman with a wife; the definition is 'Duke' alone, the jazz bandleader Duke Ellington, and the 's is just 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: Duke Ellington was the American jazz composer and bandleader.

entries.clue: Soldiers look round for protection from sun (7)

indicatorNotes.round: to turn round is to face the other way, so LO is written back to front

blocks.note: lo = look!, as in 'lo and behold'

annotation.surface: Soldiers hunt around for somewhere shady.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Look round' reads as searching; it is LO turned round.
annotation.definitionFit: A parasol is a light umbrella that shades you from the sun.

entries.clue: Suggest annuities should be reviewed (9)

indicatorNotes.should be reviewed: the letters are looked over again and rearranged

annotation.surface: A financial adviser proposes that a client's annuities be looked at again.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is sober financial advice; 'reviewed' is the only signal that ANNUITIES is to be reworked.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with a shade: to insinuate is to hint at something unpleasant without saying it outright.

entries.clue: Bachelor I saw embracing creature of the night (5)

indicatorNotes.embracing: the phrase holds the answer within it

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of 'bachelor', through 'I', into the start of 'saw'

annotation.surface: A single man recalls seeing someone hugging a nocturnal figure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bachelor' wants to be B or BA; it is only there to supply its last three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The loris is a small nocturnal primate of South and Southeast Asia.

entries.clue: Game of those coming too close to you? (5,8)

annotation.definition: Game of those coming too close to you?

blocks.note: read as any pastime, and meant as the 1978 arcade shoot-'em-up with rows of descending aliens

blocks.clueFragment: of those coming too close to you?
blocks.note: people who stand too close are invading your personal space

annotation.surface: A game about people who stand uncomfortably close.
annotation.walkthrough: People who come too close invade your personal space; Space Invaders is the 1978 arcade game of descending aliens.
annotation.definitionFit: Space Invaders is a classic video game, and space invaders are people who crowd you.

entries.clue: Aim only to come back on time (5)

blocks.note: reversal indicator: coming back means reading SOLE + T from right to left

annotation.surface: Someone's only aim is to return on time.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole of 'only ... on time' is built first, SOLE + T, and then read backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Telos, from Greek, is an ultimate end or aim.

entries.clue: You’re visiting one Asian country or another (9)

annotation.definitionNote: 'another' stands for 'another Asian country', borrowing the noun from the wordplay

indicatorNotes.visiting: a visitor is inside the place visited

blocks.note: India; ONES goes between IND and IA

annotation.surface: A traveller is told they are touring one Asian country or another.
annotation.walkthrough: One's is the formal, impersonal way of saying 'you are', as in 'one's never too old'. The first country is split open to let it in.
annotation.definitionFit: Indonesia is another Asian country, the archipelago nation south of Southeast Asia.

entries.clue: Thrilled to acquire Tesla, perhaps in August (8)

blocks.note: elated = thrilled; EV goes between EL and ATED
a Tesla is an EV, an electric vehicle

annotation.surface: Someone is delighted to buy a Tesla during the month of August.
annotation.walkthrough: 'August' at the end of the clue has a capital only because it pretends to be the month; the definition is the adjective august, grand and dignified.
annotation.definitionFit: August means majestic or lofty, which is what elevated means of style or rank.

entries.clue: Facelift going wrong, daughter distressed (9)

indicatorNotes.going wrong: the letters go astray from their proper order

annotation.surface: A cosmetic operation goes badly and the patient's daughter is upset.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface places 'going wrong' between FACELIFT and D, and it acts on both.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: someone afflicted is troubled by pain or grief, which leaves them distressed.

entries.clue: British pulling out of engagement with European PM (6)

blocks.note: an engagement is a battle; B for British is removed, leaving ATTLE
B = British, pulled out of BATTLE

annotation.surface: Britain withdraws from an engagement with a European prime minister.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Engagement' suggests diplomacy or marriage; it is a military one. Clement Attlee was the British Prime Minister from 1945 to 1951.
annotation.definitionFit: Clement Attlee was the Labour Prime Minister who followed Churchill.

entries.clue: A help getting into Oxford? (8)

blocks.note: read as a leg-up with a university application, and meant as a tool that eases a foot in
read as the university, and meant as an oxford, a laced leather shoe

annotation.surface: Someone is helped to win a place at Oxford University.
annotation.walkthrough: An oxford is also a laced leather shoe, and a shoehorn helps your heel slide in. To shoehorn someone in is also to squeeze them into a place.
annotation.definitionFit: A shoehorn is the curved tool that eases a foot into a shoe such as an oxford.

entries.clue: Time away after extremely lame excuse (3,3)

indicatorNotes.extremely: take only the extremes, first and last letters, of 'lame'
indicatorNotes.after: 'after' puts T and OFF behind LE in reading order, the way one thing follows another

blocks.note: away = off, as in a day off

annotation.surface: Someone takes time off work with a feeble excuse.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lame excuse' is a ready-made phrase, but 'excuse' is the definition as a verb and 'lame' only lends its ends.
annotation.definitionFit: To let someone off is to excuse them from a punishment or duty.

entries.clue: Suspicion surrounding Cockney woman’s patio (7)

indicatorNotes.surrounding: to surround something is to be on all sides of it, so TRACE opens up to enclose the woman's letters

blocks.note: a suspicion = a trace, a tiny amount; 'ER goes between T and RACE
her, as a Cockney says it, dropping the H

annotation.surface: A Cockney woman's patio is under suspicion.
annotation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a working-class Londoner, whose accent drops the H of 'her'. 'Suspicion' here is 'a suspicion of garlic', a trace.
annotation.definitionFit: A terrace is a paved area beside a house, a patio.

entries.clue: Two friends mostly in good health (4-4)

annotation.definitionNote: 'in good health' is a toast, as in drinking to someone's health; CHIN-CHIN is that toast

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of each word, losing its last letter

blocks.note: china = friend, from rhyming slang china plate = mate; mostly loses the A
the second of the two friends

annotation.surface: A couple of friends are for the most part healthy.
annotation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate, so a china is a friend. 'Two' asks for CHIN twice.
annotation.definitionFit: Chin-chin is a toast, like 'good health!' when raising a glass.

entries.clue: Great performances from fantastic English choirs (7)

indicatorNotes.fantastic: the letters are made fantastic, rearranged

annotation.surface: English choirs give superb concerts.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fantastic' reads as praise for the choirs; it tells you to rearrange E and CHOIRS.
annotation.definitionFit: Heroics are great, bold deeds or displays.

entries.clue: Enemy not far away, according to Spooner? Certainly not (2,4)

indicatorNotes.according to Spooner: Rev. Spooner swapped the first sounds of words

blocks.note: Spooner's slip swaps the opening sounds of the two words

annotation.surface: The enemy is close by, but someone insists all is well.
annotation.walkthrough: 'No fear!' is informal British for 'certainly not!', a flat refusal.
annotation.definitionFit: 'No fear!' is a British way of saying 'certainly not'.

entries.clue: Rome row is terribly perturbing (9)

indicatorNotes.terribly: the letters are in a terrible state, rearranged

annotation.surface: A political quarrel in Rome is deeply unsettling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Terribly perturbing' reads as one phrase, but 'terribly' works backwards on the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Worrisome means causing worry, perturbing.

entries.clue: Court appearance rebounding on copper (5)

indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, the reversed AIR comes after CU

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
an air = an appearance, as in 'an air of confidence'

annotation.surface: A police officer's court appearance goes badly for him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Copper' invites a police officer; it is the metal, Cu.
annotation.definitionFit: The Curia is the papal court of the Vatican, and in Rome a curia was a court.

entries.clue: Make out one is enthralled by tight-lipped individual (5)

indicatorNotes.is enthralled by: 'enthralled' first meant enslaved, held captive, so the one is held inside the clam

blocks.note: a clam, someone who clams up; I goes between CLA and M

annotation.surface: Someone asserts that they are captivated by a person of few words.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Make out' has several senses; here it means to assert, as in 'he made out he was ill'.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to make out that something is true is to assert it, as in 'he made out he was ill'.

entries.clue: Criticise nonsense written about American head of state (5)

indicatorNotes.written about: ROT is set down around the other letters

blocks.note: rot = nonsense; AS goes between RO and T

annotation.surface: Someone attacks the nonsense published about the US president.
annotation.walkthrough: 'American head of state' reads as the president; it splits into A and S.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: a roast is a fierce ribbing, as at a comedy roast, so the verb means to criticise harshly.

entries.clue: Haunting conclusion to homicide case (9)

blocks.note: the vocative is a grammatical case, used to address someone

annotation.surface: A murder investigation reaches a chilling end.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Case' belongs to the murder story in the surface; it is the grammatical case of Latin lessons.
annotation.definitionFit: Something evocative calls up memories or feelings, as haunting music does.

entries.clue: One conducting German songs in recital (6)

indicatorNotes.in recital: a recital is heard, so the word is judged by its sound

annotation.surface: A conductor directs a programme of German songs in concert.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Recital' fits the musical surface, and doubles as the sign that LIEDER is to be said rather than spelt.
annotation.definitionFit: A leader conducts, leading others along, as a bandleader does.

entries.clue: Last of counter-intelligence employees turned — MI6’s downfall? (7)

blocks.note: MI6 is the SIS, the Secret Intelligence Service

annotation.surface: Staff who turn double agent bring about the ruin of British intelligence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned' suggests agents turned by the enemy, fitting the spy story; it only reverses MEN. MI6 is Britain's foreign intelligence service, officially the SIS.
annotation.definitionFit: Nemesis was the Greek goddess of retribution, so the word came to mean the ruin that someone's own deeds bring on them.
